lessons.topic: Separation of Mixtures and Purification of Chemical Substances
lessons.title: Separation of Mixtures and Purification of Chemical Substances — Self-Tutoring Lesson
lessons.html:
This lesson follows the JAMB Chemistry syllabus focus for Separation of Mixtures and Purification of Chemical Substances. Start by asking whether the sample is a pure substance or a mixture. Then identify the physical property that differs between components. Use filtration for an insoluble solid in a liquid, distillation for liquids with different boiling points, crystallization for a dissolved solid, sublimation for a sublimable solid, chromatography for components that move differently with a solvent, magnetization for magnetic material, and decantation when phases can be poured apart.

Syllabus coverage

pure and impure substances; boiling and melting points; elements, compounds and mixtures; physical and chemical changes; evaporation; simple and fractional distillation; sublimation; filtration; crystallization; paper and column chromatography; magnetization; decantation

Learning objectives

  • Explain the key ideas in Separation of Mixtures and Purification of Chemical Substances in your own words.
  • Use the relevant chemical relationships, definitions and observations to solve unfamiliar questions.
  • Work through examples step by step before attempting the practice questions.
  • Check mistakes against the explanation instead of memorizing the option letter.

How to study

  1. Read the overview slowly.
  2. Copy each worked example into your notebook and solve it before reading the answer.
  3. Say the rule aloud and explain why it works.
  4. Attempt the practice questions without looking at the explanation first.
  5. Review every wrong answer and retry it later.

Worked examples

Example 1: salt water

Solution: Evaporate the water or crystallize the salt because the salt is dissolved and is not removed by filtration.

Why: The method depends on solubility and volatility.

Example 2: ethanol and water

Solution: Use fractional distillation because the liquids have different but relatively close boiling points.

Why: Fractional distillation gives repeated vaporization-condensation steps.

Example 3: iron filings and sulphur

Solution: Use magnetization to remove the magnetic iron filings.

Why: A magnetic property provides the separation principle.

Common mistakes

  • Choosing an answer because it sounds familiar without checking the chemical principle.
  • Skipping units or conditions in numerical questions.
  • Confusing similar terms such as oxidation/reduction or saturated/unsaturated.
  • Memorizing an equation without understanding what each symbol represents.

Self-test checkpoint

After this lesson, you should be able to explain the main ideas of Separation of Mixtures and Purification of Chemical Substances, solve a new example, and justify your answer.

lessons.title: Chemical Combination — Self-Tutoring Lesson
lessons.html:
This lesson follows the JAMB Chemistry syllabus focus for Chemical Combination. Chemical combination is the quantitative language of chemistry. Learn how formulas represent composition, how equations conserve atoms, and how the mole connects microscopic particles to measurable mass and volume. Always balance an equation before doing stoichiometric calculations.

Syllabus coverage

laws of definite proportions, multiple proportions, conservation of matter, Gay-Lussac combining volumes, Avogadro law; symbols, formulae and equations; relative atomic mass; mole concept and Avogadro number; stoichiometry

Learning objectives

  • Explain the key ideas in Chemical Combination in your own words.
  • Use the relevant chemical relationships, definitions and observations to solve unfamiliar questions.
  • Work through examples step by step before attempting the practice questions.
  • Check mistakes against the explanation instead of memorizing the option letter.

How to study

  1. Read the overview slowly.
  2. Copy each worked example into your notebook and solve it before reading the answer.
  3. Say the rule aloud and explain why it works.
  4. Attempt the practice questions without looking at the explanation first.
  5. Review every wrong answer and retry it later.

Worked examples

Example 1: 2 mol H2 + 1 mol O2 -> 2 mol H2O

Solution: The mole ratio is 2:1:2.

Why: Coefficients in a balanced equation give the reacting mole ratio.

Example 2: 18 g H2O

Solution: Using Mr(H2O) = 18, 18 g is 1 mol.

Why: Moles = mass / molar mass.

Example 3: CO2 composition

Solution: One carbon atom combines with two oxygen atoms in each CO2 molecule.

Why: The formula gives the fixed atomic ratio.

Common mistakes

  • Choosing an answer because it sounds familiar without checking the chemical principle.
  • Skipping units or conditions in numerical questions.
  • Confusing similar terms such as oxidation/reduction or saturated/unsaturated.
  • Memorizing an equation without understanding what each symbol represents.

Self-test checkpoint

After this lesson, you should be able to explain the main ideas of Chemical Combination, solve a new example, and justify your answer.

lessons.title: Kinetic Theory of Matter and Gas Laws — Self-Tutoring Lesson
lessons.html:
This lesson follows the JAMB Chemistry syllabus focus for Kinetic Theory of Matter and Gas Laws. Use particle motion to explain states of matter and gas behavior. For calculations, first identify the law and keep temperature in kelvin when required. Boyle relates pressure and volume at constant temperature; Charles relates volume and absolute temperature at constant pressure; the ideal gas equation links P, V, n and T.

Syllabus coverage

kinetic theory; melting, vaporization, boiling, freezing and condensation; Brownian movement; Boyle, Charles, Graham and Dalton laws; combined gas law; molar volume; atomicity; ideal gas equation PV = nRT; vapour density and relative molecular mass

Learning objectives

  • Explain the key ideas in Kinetic Theory of Matter and Gas Laws in your own words.
  • Use the relevant chemical relationships, definitions and observations to solve unfamiliar questions.
  • Work through examples step by step before attempting the practice questions.
  • Check mistakes against the explanation instead of memorizing the option letter.

How to study

  1. Read the overview slowly.
  2. Copy each worked example into your notebook and solve it before reading the answer.
  3. Say the rule aloud and explain why it works.
  4. Attempt the practice questions without looking at the explanation first.
  5. Review every wrong answer and retry it later.

Worked examples

Example 1: Boyle law

Solution: At constant temperature, P is inversely proportional to V.

Why: PV is constant for a fixed amount of gas at constant temperature.

Example 2: Charles law

Solution: At constant pressure, V is directly proportional to absolute temperature.

Why: V/T is constant.

Example 3: ideal gas

Solution: Use PV = nRT when pressure, volume, amount and temperature are related.

Why: This equation combines the basic gas variables.

Common mistakes

  • Choosing an answer because it sounds familiar without checking the chemical principle.
  • Skipping units or conditions in numerical questions.
  • Confusing similar terms such as oxidation/reduction or saturated/unsaturated.
  • Memorizing an equation without understanding what each symbol represents.

Self-test checkpoint

After this lesson, you should be able to explain the main ideas of Kinetic Theory of Matter and Gas Laws, solve a new example, and justify your answer.

lessons.title: Atomic Structure and Bonding — Self-Tutoring Lesson
lessons.html:
This lesson follows the JAMB Chemistry syllabus focus for Atomic Structure and Bonding. Build the atom from protons, neutrons and electrons. Atomic number identifies the element; mass number is protons plus neutrons. Then connect electron arrangement to periodic position and bonding. For simple molecules, learn the standard shapes named in the syllabus. Radioactivity involves unstable nuclei and different radiation types.

Syllabus coverage

atoms, molecules and ions; Dalton, Millikan, Rutherford, Moseley, Thompson and Bohr; atomic number, mass number and isotopes; electron configuration for atomic numbers 1 to 20; s and p orbitals; periodicity; ionization energy, ionic radius, electron affinity, electronegativity; ionic, covalent, coordinate, metallic and hydrogen bonding; molecular shapes; radioactivity and nuclear reactions

Learning objectives

  • Explain the key ideas in Atomic Structure and Bonding in your own words.
  • Use the relevant chemical relationships, definitions and observations to solve unfamiliar questions.
  • Work through examples step by step before attempting the practice questions.
  • Check mistakes against the explanation instead of memorizing the option letter.

How to study

  1. Read the overview slowly.
  2. Copy each worked example into your notebook and solve it before reading the answer.
  3. Say the rule aloud and explain why it works.
  4. Attempt the practice questions without looking at the explanation first.
  5. Review every wrong answer and retry it later.

Worked examples

Example 1: Na, atomic number 11

Solution: A neutral sodium atom has 11 electrons.

Why: A neutral atom has equal numbers of protons and electrons.

Example 2: CH4 shape

Solution: Tetrahedral.

Why: Four bonding pairs around carbon arrange approximately tetrahedrally.

Example 3: NaCl bonding

Solution: Ionic/electrovalent bonding.

Why: Sodium transfers an electron to chlorine, forming oppositely charged ions.

Common mistakes

  • Choosing an answer because it sounds familiar without checking the chemical principle.
  • Skipping units or conditions in numerical questions.
  • Confusing similar terms such as oxidation/reduction or saturated/unsaturated.
  • Memorizing an equation without understanding what each symbol represents.

Self-test checkpoint

After this lesson, you should be able to explain the main ideas of Atomic Structure and Bonding, solve a new example, and justify your answer.

lessons.title: Air — Self-Tutoring Lesson
lessons.html:
This lesson follows the JAMB Chemistry syllabus focus for Air. Air is a mixture, not a compound. Learn its major components, the role of oxygen in combustion and respiration, the relatively unreactive nature of nitrogen, and the uses of noble gases. Separation of air is based mainly on liquefaction followed by fractional distillation.

Syllabus coverage

composition of air; separation of air; oxygen and nitrogen; noble gases; air pollution; combustion; uses and laboratory preparation of oxygen and nitrogen; properties of oxygen and nitrogen

Learning objectives

  • Explain the key ideas in Air in your own words.
  • Use the relevant chemical relationships, definitions and observations to solve unfamiliar questions.
  • Work through examples step by step before attempting the practice questions.
  • Check mistakes against the explanation instead of memorizing the option letter.

How to study

  1. Read the overview slowly.
  2. Copy each worked example into your notebook and solve it before reading the answer.
  3. Say the rule aloud and explain why it works.
  4. Attempt the practice questions without looking at the explanation first.
  5. Review every wrong answer and retry it later.

Worked examples

Example 1: oxygen

Solution: Supports combustion but is not itself a fuel.

Why: A glowing splint relights in oxygen.

Example 2: nitrogen

Solution: Makes up most of the atmosphere and is relatively unreactive under ordinary conditions.

Why: Its stability is linked to the strong N2 bond.

Example 3: noble gases

Solution: They are chemically unreactive compared with many other elements.

Why: Their outer electron shells are complete.

Common mistakes

  • Choosing an answer because it sounds familiar without checking the chemical principle.
  • Skipping units or conditions in numerical questions.
  • Confusing similar terms such as oxidation/reduction or saturated/unsaturated.
  • Memorizing an equation without understanding what each symbol represents.

Self-test checkpoint

After this lesson, you should be able to explain the main ideas of Air, solve a new example, and justify your answer.

lessons.title: Water — Self-Tutoring Lesson
lessons.html:
This lesson follows the JAMB Chemistry syllabus focus for Water. Water is studied as a chemical substance, a solvent and an environmental resource. Distinguish temporary hardness, caused mainly by hydrogencarbonates, from permanent hardness, associated with sulphates and chlorides. Water treatment removes suspended matter, microbes and other unwanted substances.

Syllabus coverage

sources and properties of water; hard and soft water; temporary and permanent hardness; causes and removal of hardness; water treatment; water pollution; tests for water; industrial and domestic importance

Learning objectives

  • Explain the key ideas in Water in your own words.
  • Use the relevant chemical relationships, definitions and observations to solve unfamiliar questions.
  • Work through examples step by step before attempting the practice questions.
  • Check mistakes against the explanation instead of memorizing the option letter.

How to study

  1. Read the overview slowly.
  2. Copy each worked example into your notebook and solve it before reading the answer.
  3. Say the rule aloud and explain why it works.
  4. Attempt the practice questions without looking at the explanation first.
  5. Review every wrong answer and retry it later.

Worked examples

Example 1: temporary hardness

Solution: Boiling can remove it by decomposing hydrogencarbonates and forming insoluble material.

Why: Heating changes soluble hydrogencarbonates into less soluble products.

Example 2: hard water

Solution: It consumes more soap because insoluble scum can form.

Why: Ca2+ and Mg2+ ions interfere with soap action.

Example 3: chlorination

Solution: Chlorine is used to disinfect treated water.

Why: It helps kill harmful microorganisms.

Common mistakes

  • Choosing an answer because it sounds familiar without checking the chemical principle.
  • Skipping units or conditions in numerical questions.
  • Confusing similar terms such as oxidation/reduction or saturated/unsaturated.
  • Memorizing an equation without understanding what each symbol represents.

Self-test checkpoint

After this lesson, you should be able to explain the main ideas of Water, solve a new example, and justify your answer.

lessons.title: Solubility — Self-Tutoring Lesson
lessons.html:
This lesson follows the JAMB Chemistry syllabus focus for Solubility. Solubility tells how much solute can dissolve in a specified amount of solvent under specified conditions. Read solubility curves carefully: points on the curve represent saturation, below the curve is generally unsaturated, and crystallization can occur when a hot saturated solution cools.

Syllabus coverage

meaning of solubility; saturated, unsaturated and supersaturated solutions; solubility curves; factors affecting solubility; crystallization; calculations involving solubility; hydrated salts

Learning objectives

  • Explain the key ideas in Solubility in your own words.
  • Use the relevant chemical relationships, definitions and observations to solve unfamiliar questions.
  • Work through examples step by step before attempting the practice questions.
  • Check mistakes against the explanation instead of memorizing the option letter.

How to study

  1. Read the overview slowly.
  2. Copy each worked example into your notebook and solve it before reading the answer.
  3. Say the rule aloud and explain why it works.
  4. Attempt the practice questions without looking at the explanation first.
  5. Review every wrong answer and retry it later.

Worked examples

Example 1: saturated solution

Solution: It contains the maximum amount of dissolved solute under stated conditions.

Why: Additional solute will not dissolve under those conditions.

Example 2: cooling a hot solution

Solution: Solubility often decreases for many solids, so crystals may form.

Why: The excess solute separates as the solution becomes supersaturated.

Example 3: hydrated salt

Solution: It contains water of crystallization in its crystal structure.

Why: The water is part of the crystalline composition.

Common mistakes

  • Choosing an answer because it sounds familiar without checking the chemical principle.
  • Skipping units or conditions in numerical questions.
  • Confusing similar terms such as oxidation/reduction or saturated/unsaturated.
  • Memorizing an equation without understanding what each symbol represents.

Self-test checkpoint

After this lesson, you should be able to explain the main ideas of Solubility, solve a new example, and justify your answer.

lessons.title: Environmental Pollution — Self-Tutoring Lesson
lessons.html:
This lesson follows the JAMB Chemistry syllabus focus for Environmental Pollution. Identify the pollutant, its source, its effect and a control measure. Acid rain is strongly associated with oxides of sulphur and nitrogen. Greenhouse gases contribute to warming. Nutrient enrichment can cause eutrophication. Good answers connect a chemical cause to a measurable environmental consequence.

Syllabus coverage

pollutants; air, water and land pollution; sources and effects of pollutants; greenhouse effect; acid rain; ozone depletion; eutrophication; control of pollution; environmental protection

Learning objectives

  • Explain the key ideas in Environmental Pollution in your own words.
  • Use the relevant chemical relationships, definitions and observations to solve unfamiliar questions.
  • Work through examples step by step before attempting the practice questions.
  • Check mistakes against the explanation instead of memorizing the option letter.

How to study

  1. Read the overview slowly.
  2. Copy each worked example into your notebook and solve it before reading the answer.
  3. Say the rule aloud and explain why it works.
  4. Attempt the practice questions without looking at the explanation first.
  5. Review every wrong answer and retry it later.

Worked examples

Example 1: acid rain

Solution: Sulphur oxides and nitrogen oxides can contribute to acid rain.

Why: These gases form acidic products in atmospheric moisture.

Example 2: eutrophication

Solution: Excess nutrients can cause excessive algal growth and oxygen depletion.

Why: Decomposition of biomass consumes dissolved oxygen.

Example 3: ozone layer

Solution: Stratospheric ozone absorbs much harmful ultraviolet radiation.

Why: Ozone depletion increases UV exposure.

Common mistakes

  • Choosing an answer because it sounds familiar without checking the chemical principle.
  • Skipping units or conditions in numerical questions.
  • Confusing similar terms such as oxidation/reduction or saturated/unsaturated.
  • Memorizing an equation without understanding what each symbol represents.

Worked examples

Example 1: pH 2

Solution: This is strongly acidic.

Why: Lower pH means higher hydronium ion concentration.

Example 2: H2SO4 basicity

Solution: It is dibasic in the usual syllabus sense because it can furnish two replaceable acidic hydrogen ions.

Why: Basicity refers to the number of replaceable hydrogen ions in an acid.

Example 3: NaCl

Solution: It is a normal salt.

Why: It is formed from complete neutralization of a strong acid by a strong base.

lessons.title: Oxidation and Reduction — Self-Tutoring Lesson
lessons.html:
This lesson follows the JAMB Chemistry syllabus focus for Oxidation and Reduction. Think of redox as electron transfer. Oxidation is loss of electrons and reduction is gain of electrons. Oxidation number changes provide another way to identify redox. The oxidizing agent is reduced, while the reducing agent is oxidized.

Syllabus coverage

oxidation and reduction concepts; oxidation numbers; oxidizing and reducing agents; balancing simple redox equations; electron transfer; redox applications

Learning objectives

  • Explain the key ideas in Oxidation and Reduction in your own words.
  • Use the relevant chemical relationships, definitions and observations to solve unfamiliar questions.
  • Work through examples step by step before attempting the practice questions.

How to study

  1. Read the overview slowly.
  2. Copy each worked example into your notebook and solve it before reading the answer.
  3. Say the rule aloud and explain why it works.
  4. Attempt the practice questions without looking at the explanation first.
  5. Review every wrong answer and retry it later.

Worked examples

Example 1: oxidation

Solution: Loss of electrons or increase in oxidation number.

Why: Both descriptions identify oxidation.

Example 2: reducing agent

Solution: It donates electrons and is itself oxidized.

Why: The reducing agent causes another species to be reduced.

Example 3: Zn -> Zn2+

Solution: Zinc is oxidized.

Why: Its oxidation number increases from 0 to +2.

  • Choosing an answer because it sounds familiar without checking the chemical principle.
  • Skipping units or conditions in numerical questions.
  • Confusing similar terms such as oxidation/reduction or saturated/unsaturated.
  • Memorizing an equation without understanding what each symbol represents.

lessons.title: Electrolysis — Self-Tutoring Lesson
lessons.html:
This lesson follows the JAMB Chemistry syllabus focus for Electrolysis. Electrolysis uses electrical energy to drive a non-spontaneous chemical change. Cations move toward the cathode and anions toward the anode. In aqueous solutions, the species discharged depends on concentration, electrode nature and relative ease of discharge. Faraday laws connect charge passed with amount of substance produced.

Syllabus coverage

electrolytes and non-electrolytes; electrodes; electrolysis of molten and aqueous substances; preferential discharge; Faraday laws; electroplating; extraction and purification of metals

Learning objectives

  • Explain the key ideas in Electrolysis in your own words.
  • Use the relevant chemical relationships, definitions and observations to solve unfamiliar questions.
  • Work through examples step by step before attempting the practice questions.
  • Check mistakes against the explanation instead of memorizing the option letter.

How to study

  1. Read the overview slowly.

  3. Say the rule aloud and explain why it works.
  4. Attempt the practice questions without looking at the explanation first.
  5. Review every wrong answer and retry it later.

Worked examples

Example 1: cathode

Solution: Reduction occurs at the cathode.

Why: Remember: reduction at cathode.

Example 2: electroplating

Solution: A thin layer of a metal is deposited on an object using electrolysis.

Why: The object to be coated is connected as the cathode in the usual arrangement.

Example 3: molten NaCl

Solution: Sodium is produced at the cathode and chlorine at the anode.

Why: Na+ is reduced and Cl- is oxidized.

lessons.title: Energy Changes — Self-Tutoring Lesson
lessons.html:
This lesson follows the JAMB Chemistry syllabus focus for Energy Changes. Track energy rather than memorizing isolated words. Exothermic reactions release heat and have a negative enthalpy change under the usual convention; endothermic reactions absorb heat and have a positive enthalpy change. Energy profiles show activation energy and overall energy change.

Syllabus coverage

exothermic and endothermic reactions; energy profile; enthalpy change; heat of reaction, formation, combustion, neutralization and solution; bond energy; entropy and spontaneity at elementary level

Learning objectives

  • Explain the key ideas in Energy Changes in your own words.

How to study

  1. Read the overview slowly.

  5. Review every wrong answer and retry it later.

Worked examples

Example 1: exothermic

Solution: Heat is released to the surroundings.

Why: The products have lower enthalpy than the reactants when the reaction is exothermic.

Example 2: bond breaking

Solution: Requires energy.

Why: Energy is needed to overcome attractive forces in bonds.

Example 3: bond making

Solution: Releases energy.

Why: Formation of bonds leads to a lower-energy arrangement.

lessons.title: Rates of Chemical Reaction — Self-Tutoring Lesson
lessons.html:
This lesson follows the JAMB Chemistry syllabus focus for Rates of Chemical Reaction. A reaction is faster when effective collisions occur more frequently. Higher temperature increases particle energy and the fraction of particles above activation energy. Higher concentration, greater surface area and suitable catalysts can increase rate. Catalysts provide an alternative pathway with lower activation energy.

Syllabus coverage

rate of reaction; collision theory; activation energy; concentration, temperature, pressure, surface area and catalysts; graphs and experimental determination of rate

Learning objectives

  • Explain the key ideas in Rates of Chemical Reaction in your own words.
  • Use the relevant chemical relationships, definitions and observations to solve unfamiliar questions.
  • Work through examples step by step before attempting the practice questions.
  • Check mistakes against the explanation instead of memorizing the option letter.

How to study

  1. Read the overview slowly.
  2. Copy each worked example into your notebook and solve it before reading the answer.
  3. Say the rule aloud and explain why it works.
  4. Attempt the practice questions without looking at the explanation first.
  5. Review every wrong answer and retry it later.

Worked examples

Example 1: catalyst

Solution: It increases reaction rate without being permanently consumed overall.

Why: It lowers activation energy through an alternative pathway.

Example 2: powdered solid

Solution: It usually reacts faster than the same mass as large lumps.

Why: Powder exposes a larger surface area for collisions.

Example 3: higher temperature

Solution: Usually increases reaction rate.

Why: More particles have sufficient energy for successful collisions.

lessons.title: Chemical Equilibria — Self-Tutoring Lesson
lessons.html:
This lesson follows the JAMB Chemistry syllabus focus for Chemical Equilibria. A reversible reaction can reach dynamic equilibrium in a closed system when forward and reverse reaction rates become equal. Concentrations do not have to be equal. Use Le Chatelier principle to predict how concentration, pressure or temperature changes affect the position of equilibrium.

Syllabus coverage

reversible reactions; dynamic equilibrium; equilibrium constant at elementary level; Le Chatelier principle; effects of concentration, pressure and temperature; industrial examples

Learning objectives

  • Explain the key ideas in Chemical Equilibria in your own words.
  • Use the relevant chemical relationships, definitions and observations to solve unfamiliar questions.
  • Work through examples step by step before attempting the practice questions.
  • Check mistakes against the explanation instead of memorizing the option letter.

How to study

  1. Read the overview slowly.
  2. Copy each worked example into your notebook and solve it before reading the answer.
  3. Say the rule aloud and explain why it works.
  4. Attempt the practice questions without looking at the explanation first.
  5. Review every wrong answer and retry it later.

Worked examples

Example 1: equilibrium

Solution: Forward and reverse reactions continue at equal rates.

Why: The system is dynamic, not static.

Example 2: increase reactant concentration

Solution: The system tends to consume some of the added reactant.

Why: This shifts the equilibrium toward products in a simple case.

Example 3: increase pressure

Solution: For gaseous equilibria, the system tends to favor the side with fewer gas molecules.

Why: The pressure change is opposed by shifting toward fewer gas particles.

  • Skipping units or conditions in numerical questions.

  • Memorizing an equation without understanding what each symbol represents.

lessons.title: Organic Compounds — Self-Tutoring Lesson
lessons.html:
This lesson follows the JAMB Chemistry syllabus focus for Organic Compounds. Organic chemistry becomes easier when you classify compounds by functional group and homologous series. Learn general formulae, IUPAC naming, structural isomerism, reactions and uses. Connect petroleum fractions to boiling range and uses, and distinguish addition from condensation polymerization.

Syllabus coverage

tetravalency and catenation; IUPAC nomenclature; empirical formula; alkanes, alkenes, alkynes and benzene; petroleum, cracking and reforming; alkanols; alkanals and alkanones; alkanoic acids and alkanoates; amines; carbohydrates; proteins; fats and oils; polymers

Learning objectives

  • Explain the key ideas in Organic Compounds in your own words.
  • Use the relevant chemical relationships, definitions and observations to solve unfamiliar questions.
  • Work through examples step by step before attempting the practice questions.
  • Check mistakes against the explanation instead of memorizing the option letter.

How to study

  1. Read the overview slowly.
  2. Copy each worked example into your notebook and solve it before reading the answer.
  3. Say the rule aloud and explain why it works.
  4. Attempt the practice questions without looking at the explanation first.
  5. Review every wrong answer and retry it later.

Worked examples

Example 1: alkanes

Solution: They are saturated hydrocarbons containing only single carbon-carbon bonds.

Why: Their general formula for open-chain members is CnH2n+2.

Example 2: alkenes

Solution: They contain a carbon-carbon double bond and undergo addition reactions.

Why: The pi component of the double bond permits addition.

Example 3: ethanoic acid

Solution: It is an alkanoic acid with the functional group -COOH.

Why: Carboxylic acids contain the carboxyl group.

Common mistakes

  • Choosing an answer because it sounds familiar without checking the chemical principle.
  • Skipping units or conditions in numerical questions.
  • Confusing similar terms such as oxidation/reduction or saturated/unsaturated.
  • Memorizing an equation without understanding what each symbol represents.

Self-test checkpoint

After this lesson, you should be able to explain the main ideas of Organic Compounds, solve a new example, and justify your answer.

lessons.title: Chemistry and Industry — Self-Tutoring Lesson
lessons.html:
This lesson follows the JAMB Chemistry syllabus focus for Chemistry and Industry. Industrial chemistry asks three questions: what is the raw material, what process changes it, and why is the product useful? Distinguish heavy chemicals from fine chemicals and connect industrial chemistry to agriculture, construction, fuels, medicines and biotechnology.

Syllabus coverage

chemical industries; raw materials; fine and heavy chemicals; relevance of industries; fertilizers, cement, petroleum and other industrial processes; biotechnology

Learning objectives

  • Explain the key ideas in Chemistry and Industry in your own words.
  • Use the relevant chemical relationships, definitions and observations to solve unfamiliar questions.
  • Work through examples step by step before attempting the practice questions.
  • Check mistakes against the explanation instead of memorizing the option letter.

How to study

  1. Read the overview slowly.
  2. Copy each worked example into your notebook and solve it before reading the answer.
  3. Say the rule aloud and explain why it works.
  4. Attempt the practice questions without looking at the explanation first.
  5. Review every wrong answer and retry it later.

Worked examples

Example 1: cement

Solution: Limestone is a major raw material in cement manufacture.

Why: Calcareous material supplies much of the calcium-containing component.

Example 2: fertilizer industry

Solution: Ammonia is a key starting material for several nitrogen fertilizers.

Why: Ammonia supplies nitrogen in industrial fertilizer chemistry.

Example 3: biotechnology

Solution: Uses biological systems or organisms to make useful products or processes.

Why: It links chemistry with controlled biological activity.

  • Confusing similar terms such as oxidation/reduction or saturated/unsaturated.
  • Memorizing an equation without understanding what each symbol represents.
